requirement: Split any iterable into fixed-size tuples lazily, keeping or dropping a short tail on request, and produce full-width sliding windows, rejecting sizes below one.
skeleton: chunked generator built on islice over one shared iterator with a drop_partial flag, and sliding generator built on a bounded deque.
caption: Two lazy standard-library generators for grouping a stream. chunked(items, size, drop_partial=False) raises ValueError saying size must be at least 1 when size is below one, takes a single iterator over the input, and repeatedly pulls a tuple of up to size items with itertools.islice until an empty tuple comes back; when drop_partial is set and the last tuple is shorter than size it stops instead of yielding it. Because it works from one shared iterator it never materializes the input and works on infinite streams. sliding(items, width) raises ValueError saying width must be at least 1 for a width below one, keeps a collections.deque bounded to width, appends each item, and yields the deque as a tuple only once it holds exactly width items, so inputs shorter than the width produce nothing. Both are generic over the element type. The fixture asserts that range(7) in threes gives (0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5) and (6,), that drop_partial removes only a short tail, that the first chunk of itertools.count arrives without exhausting it, that a size of zero raises ValueError, that windows of three over abcd are abc and bcd while ab yields none, and that a width of zero raises ValueError.

plan.intent: Group a stream into chunks and windows lazily
constraints: Chunks are tuples of the requested size taken from one iterator
The short tail is kept by default and dropped only on request
Windows are yielded only at full width
Sizes and widths below one raise ValueError

rationale.teaches: islice over a single iterator with a walrus loop, and a maxlen deque for sliding windows.
rationale.why: Chunking code commonly gets the tail policy, the tuple type or the window start wrong, and each mistake only shows at the edge of the input, so fixed small ranges expose them exactly.

ops.docstring: Split iterables into fixed-size chunks and sliding windows lazily.

candidates.why_wrong: A zero chunk size silently yields nothing instead of raising ValueError.
The tail test is inverted, so the short tail is dropped by default and kept when dropping was requested.
Chunks are built as lists, so they never compare equal to the expected tuples.
Windows start one item early, so a partial window is yielded before the first full one.
drop_partial defaults to true, so the trailing partial chunk disappears unless the caller opts out.
